entries.looks_like: The figures 925 struck in a small oblong punch, beside a maker's mark and, depending on the country, other marks.
entries.means: The metal is stated to be 925 parts silver in 1000: sterling. Struck by an assay office in the UK (where the number sits in a shield); stamped by the maker in the US and in Germany, where the law holds the maker to it.
entries.date_note: No single start date: each country's law sets when the number could be used (Germany from 1888; the UK number-in-shield mark is in british-hallmarks.json).

sources.where: Sched. 2: silver 925, standard mark the figures 925

§§ 2–3: fineness stated in thousandths, 800 or more
p. 19: the old standard of 11 oz 2 dwt in the pound troy (= 925/1000)

entries.looks_like: The figures 800 struck in a small punch; in Germany from 1888 beside a crescent moon and a crown.
entries.means: The metal is stated to be 800 parts silver in 1000. It is the lowest UK standard for silver and the lowest fineness German law let a maker state on silver wares from 1888.
entries.date_note: Germany: stated fineness on silver wares only at 800 or more, from 1 January 1888.

visual.note: On this fork the crescent, crown and 800 share one punch outline; the crop takes only the 800 part. The maker's star is left out.

entries.looks_like: The figures 900 struck in a small punch, sometimes written as a fraction, 900 over 1000. Shown here as set in type in Ensko's 1915 list of marks, beside F. W. Cooper's name mark (W. Cooper).
entries.means: The metal is stated to be 900 parts silver in 1000, the US coin standard from 1837; in the US an item marked COIN must meet it.

entries.name: STERLING
entries.looks_like: The word STERLING (sometimes STER.) stamped in plain capitals, usually beside the maker's mark. Shown here as set in type in the 1922 Jewelers' Circular trade-marks book, above D. D. Codding's D. D. C. mark.
entries.means: The maker states the metal is at least 925 parts silver in 1000. Since 1906 US law forbids the word on anything below 925, and on plate.
entries.date_note: Sources differ on the start: French (1917) about 1857; Kovels (1989) frequently used by 1860; Yale and Rainwater (2004) the 1860s, Rainwater 'not used consistently' until about 1865.

sources.where: (b)(2) and note 1 (15 U.S.C. 297(a): not on plated wares)
glossary: 'About 1857 the word Sterling was stamped on silver articles'
introduction: sterling standard by the 1860s
p. vii: the word STERLING was frequently used by 1860; STERLING means 925 out of 1000 parts silver
p. 309, glossary 'Sterling Silver: 925/1000 fine'; p. 311, table: .925 not used consistently in the US (outside Baltimore) until c. 1865
p. 125: D. D. Codding, North Attleboro: STERLING over D. D. C.

disagreements.note: 'not used consistently elsewhere in the U.S. until c. 1865'

visual.credit: As set in type in The Jewelers' Circular, Trade-Marks of the Jewelry and Kindred Trades (1922), p. 125, public domain.
visual.note: Type, not a cut of the punch: plain capitals, as the word is usually struck. The D. D. C. line below is left out.

entries.name: COIN
entries.looks_like: The word COIN in plain capitals, unframed, struck beside an early American maker's mark.
entries.means: The maker states the metal is of the standard of US silver coin: 892.4/1000 before 1837, 900/1000 after. Since 1906 US law requires 900 for the word.
entries.date_note: Mostly before the 1860s; French dates the word's use to after 1837.

sources.where: glossary: 'Coin — This word stamped by a die on silver after 1837 designated that the metal was of the same fineness as silver money'

entries.name: PURE COIN
entries.looks_like: The words PURE COIN (or PURE SILVER COIN) beside an American maker's mark. Shown here as set in type in Ensko's 1915 list of marks, for Vincent Laforme & Brother of Boston (Pure Coin / V. L. & B. / Boston).
entries.means: As COIN: the maker states the metal is of the US silver coin standard. Seen on New England silver.
entries.date_note: By 1830 (Kovels; Rainwater) until the move to sterling in the 1860s.

Photo lead (not used): NMAH prize cup DL*60.0990 (record ld1-1643398853934-1643398864738-0), underside struck PURE COIN in a triangle; its CC0 base photo (NMAH-AHB2014q060853) shows the mark only as a sliver between two paper labels, so no clean crop. A new photograph with the labels lifted would serve; ask NMAH.

entries.name: STANDARD
entries.looks_like: The word STANDARD stamped beside an American maker's mark, sometimes in a scroll.
entries.means: The maker states the metal is of the coin (dollar) standard. Found on silver made around Philadelphia.
entries.date_note: By 1830 (Kovels; Rainwater) until the move to sterling in the 1860s.

searched: Wikimedia Commons: Category:Hallmarks and its country subcategories, Category:Nickel silver, Category:Silver plating hallmarks, and keyword searches (2026-11-22)
The Met Open Access: collection API returned 410 Gone and the website refused automated fetching (2026-11-22), so Met mark images could not be searched

Jewelers' Circular, Trade-Marks of the Jewelry and Kindred Trades (1896), archive.org: read all 220 pages' OCR and checked candidates on the page images: STANDARD appears only in plate trade names (STANDARD PLATE) and firm names, not as the coin-standard mark.

Not reached: the 1904 and 1915 editions (not found on archive.org; HathiTrust not tried) and Rosenberg, Der Goldschmiede Merkzeichen (1911, 1922), which covers European goldsmiths' marks before about 1850 and isn't likely to show these American words.

Jewelers' Circular, Trade-Marks of the Jewelry and Kindred Trades (1922), HathiTrust hvd.hb9jsx, scans 146–220 (silverware and plated ware), read with on-device OCR and checked by eye: STANDARD appears only in plate names (STANDARD PLATE), a firm name (Standard Silver Co.) and watch grades, not as the coin-standard mark.
Kovels' American Silver Marks (1989) and Rainwater's Encyclopedia (2004) are in copyright: cited for facts only, images not reproduced.

Ensko, Makers of Early American Silver (1915) and American Silversmiths and Their Marks (1927); French (1917); archive.org full-text search of pre-1929 texts for 'stamped standard' and 'marked standard': no STANDARD mark set in type or drawn.

Cleveland Museum of Art open access API (CC0), 2026-11-24: 'standard silver', 'coin silver', 'pure coin', and ~140 silver spoons, ladles, cups and hollowware filtered for STANDARD, COIN, DOLLAR or PREMIUM in their inscriptions: only Russian '88 silver standard' marks, no American STANDARD.

Flickr search (in the browser; the open-licence filter returned an error without a login, so licences were checked on each photo page) and Wikimedia Commons full-text searches, 2026-11-24: 'coin silver spoon', 'Philadelphia silver spoon mark', 'silversmith mark "STANDARD"', 'insource:"coin silver" standard'. Nearest: 'Silver Berry Spoon.jpg' (Peter L. Krider, Philadelphia; public domain via DPLA), front view only, no mark shown.
Openverse API, 2026-11-24: refused anonymous requests (429, then 401 Unauthorized), so not searched.

Smithsonian Open Access API with a registered key, 2026-11-24: 'spoon', 'teaspoon', 'coin silver', 'silver Philadelphia', 'silver Baltimore', 'silver tablespoon', 'silver fork', 'silver ladle', 'silver beaker', 'silver cup', 'sugar tongs', 'silversmith mark' (up to 1000 records each), records with CC0 images and their mark descriptions read. Found: National Museum of American History child's cup (record ld1-1643398853934-1643398857126-1), underside struck 'STANDARD' and two other marks, but the record has no online images. Ask: NMAH (Smithsonian) for a photograph of the underside. Also seen: Peter L. Krider's coin silver presentation pitcher, Philadelphia 1851 (NMAH 2005.0233.0915, 6 CC0 images), no view of its marks.

Joe Haupt's Flickr (CC BY-SA 2.0), 2026-11-24: the public tag feed returned nothing for coinsilver, antiquesilver, vintagesilver, silverspoon, hallmark, standard and similar tags (his tags are long compound phrases); his Commons mirror searched instead: 28 coin silver pocket-watch photos, case lids checked; the readable lid stamps are watch-case makers' marks (e.g. Am. Watch Co. Waltham, WARRANTED COIN SILVER), no STANDARD.

Google Images with the Creative Commons filter (in the browser), 2026-11-24: 'coin silver spoon mark' and '"STANDARD" coin silver spoon mark': coins, Cleveland's Erastus Cook tablespoon (front view) and LACMA teaspoons (front views); no STANDARD mark.

entries.name: Crescent moon and crown
entries.looks_like: A crescent moon with a crown to its right, often in one shaped punch, struck beside the fineness number (800 or more) and the maker's mark.
entries.means: German silver ware of the stated fineness (at least 800), marked under the German Empire's law of 1884. The crescent stands for silver, the crown for the Reich. Not used on jewelry.
entries.date_note: From 1 January 1888; the end date isn't in these sources.

sources.where: the mark: Reichskrone, Mondsichel for silver, fineness in thousandths, the firm's mark; crown to the right of the crescent

entries.name: NICKEL SILVER
entries.looks_like: The words NICKEL SILVER stamped in capitals, here over a second line, WEAR-WHITE, in the same punch.
entries.means: The item is nickel silver (German silver): an alloy of copper, nickel and zinc with no silver in it.
entries.date_note: The US Bureau of Standards noted in 1921 that the trade had moved from 'German silver' to 'nickel silver' after the war.

sources.where: whole entry

disagreements.note: Composition: Bureau of Standards, copper 52–80%, zinc 10–35%, nickel 5–30%; Meyers, brass with 16–33% nickel (usually 25%).

visual.credit: Photograph: Smirkybec, Nickel silver teaspoon marks.jpg, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0; cropped and toned by Heirloom.
visual.note: WEAR-WHITE is the second line of the same punch, read as a trade name; the number 12 and the maker's oval are left out.

entries.means: Alpacca (Alpaka): nickel silver, by the photographer's description; Meyers gives Alpaka as a name for silver-plated nickel silver. Either way the body has no silver.

entries.date_note: Bureau of Standards (1921): the usual name until the trade moved to 'nickel silver' after the war.

entries.name: EPNS
entries.looks_like: The letters EPNS (sometimes E.P.N.S.) stamped in capitals, often with the maker's mark and a pattern or quality mark.
entries.means: Electroplated nickel silver: a nickel silver body with a thin coat of silver laid on by electroplating. The silver is only on the surface.
